title: Who pays and who saves: auto-enrolment, low earners and the state pension
label: 11 November 2026 · Pensions adequacy inquiry
summary: The Committee questioned experts and campaigners on how auto-enrolment should support low earners. Witnesses agreed the UK needs clearer adequacy goals: avoid pensioner poverty and smooth lifetime living standards. They warned the Government’s adjustment to the triple lock increases pressure on private saving, making higher automatic contributions (Pensions UK’s 8%→12%) urgent. But raising defaults risks hurting low earners now; the witnesses discussed uprating thresholds, better sequencing, employer support, and mitigations such as non-contingent employer contributions, small accessible “sidecar” savings, and targeted help for women and the self-employed.

glossary.definition: A system that automatically signs employees into workplace pensions unless they opt out.
The rule that annual State Pension increases are the highest of inflation, average earnings growth, or 2.5%.
The UK government pension paid to people who reach State Pension age with sufficient National Insurance records.
A cash threshold below which earnings are not counted for auto-enrolment or certain pension entitlements.
A cash threshold above which an employee is automatically enrolled into a workplace pension by their employer.
A means-tested benefit that top-ups the incomes of very low-income pensioners.
A means-tested benefit for people of working age on low incomes.

chapters.title: What should pension adequacy mean?
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses agreed adequacy has two aims: prevent pensioner poverty and smooth people’s living standards between working life and retirement.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Pensions Commission asks what adequacy objectives should be for low earners. What should we aim to deliver?

turns.speaker: Carl Emmerson
turns.text: Two clear objectives: avoid widespread pensioner poverty and help people smooth living standards so retirement doesn't leave them much worse off than work.

turns.speaker: Chris Curry
turns.text: I agree. For low earners a minimum standard that lets people participate in society is crucial. Measures must also reflect needs like housing or disability costs.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Cribb
turns.text: A hybrid metric can help—combining a minimum standard and replacement rates—but be careful mixing different concepts. We should also watch how minimum standards compare to working-age incomes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should periodic, holistic reviews be built into pensions policy?

turns.speaker: Chris Curry
turns.text: Yes—independent, regular reviews help. They don’t have to be binding, but should clarify the objectives and act as an early-warning system.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Cribb
turns.text: Periodic reviews every 10–15 years are sensible: they give stability but let policy catch up with big changes.

chapters.title: Triple lock change tightens the private saving task
chapters.takeaway: Adjusting the triple lock reduces the projected State Pension, so private pensions and higher contributions become more important.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How does the Government’s adjusted triple lock affect what people must save?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Cribb
turns.text: The adjustment makes the state pension more predictable but lower relative to earnings over the long run, so private saving needs to rise to make up the gap.

turns.speaker: Chris Curry
turns.text: Yes. The change clarifies the scale of the shortfall. Previous estimates show many more people may be undersaving under a less generous lock.

turns.speaker: Carl Emmerson
turns.text: Our modelling shows a median earner might need substantially higher private contributions to reach the same retirement income under the adjusted rule.

turns.speaker: Zoe Alexander
turns.text: That’s why Pensions UK urges rising auto-enrolment from 8% to 12%—the private system must do more if the state provides less.

turns.speaker: Dr Daniella Jenkins
turns.text: Women are particularly exposed: many rely mostly on the state pension and live longer, so the long-term squeeze hits them hardest, especially those born in the 1970s.

turns.speaker: Jack Jones
turns.text: A lower state pension increases the need for workplace saving and better ways to turn small pots into a secure income—collective DC and guided retirement help.

chapters.title: Raise contributions, but sequence and protect low earners
chapters.takeaway: Most witnesses back higher contribution targets, but recommend gradual timetables, employer-first funding, uprating thresholds and mitigations for low earners.

turns.speaker: Mr Peter Bedford
turns.text: Is raising contributions to 12% sensible and how should the increase be split between employer and employee?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Cribb
turns.text: Moving to around 12% on qualifying earnings makes sense, but don’t apply 12% on all earnings without care. Allow options for lower contributions so people can stay in with an employer contribution.

turns.speaker: Chris Curry
turns.text: Higher contributions are justified, but implementation matters. Employers can absorb costs if given long notice; historically, increases were phased in over many years.

turns.speaker: Carl Emmerson
turns.text: Automatic enrolment works. The issue is we still lack enough voluntary saving. Raise defaults gradually, give long notice, and consider wage dynamics and the national living wage when timing increases.

turns.speaker: Jack Jones
turns.text: Put more of the rise onto employers where possible—international norms and fairness suggest employers should bear a bigger share, and it reduces pressure on low earners’ take-home pay.

turns.speaker: Zoe Alexander
turns.text: Pensions UK proposes a path to 12% by the early 2030s with employer contributions rising first. But we must examine the lower earnings limit and the earnings trigger carefully.

turns.speaker: John Milne
turns.text: If we lower the lower earnings limit to zero, how do we protect people who genuinely can’t afford to divert pay into pensions?

turns.speaker: Will Sandbrook
turns.text: Mitigations include allowing opt-downs without losing employer contributions, non-contingent employer payments, or PAESA sidecars that let a small share be accessed for emergencies.

turns.speaker: Dr Daniella Jenkins
turns.text: We must target help for women and households where increased contributions would cut already-scarce working-age resources. Repurpose some tax relief to support employers who mainly employ low paid workers.

chapters.title: Options to protect low earners
chapters.takeaway: Experts suggested practical mitigations—uprating cash thresholds, better Universal Credit alignment, employer trials of non-contingent contributions, and accessible savings linked to pensions.

turns.speaker: Patrick Hurley
turns.text: If we change thresholds or remove the LEL, what support is needed so low earners can afford extra contributions?

turns.speaker: Carl Emmerson
turns.text: Ensure eligible households get correct Universal Credit. Improve take-up and administration so UC offsets some of the cost of pension saving for low-income households.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Cribb
turns.text: Any cash thresholds like the earnings trigger and LEL should be uprated (prices or earnings). Fixed cash limits suffer fiscal drag and pull more people in over time unintentionally.

turns.speaker: Chris Curry
turns.text: Consider simple mitigations rather than many overlapping rules. Dual-account approaches, limited access to savings, or opt-downs are less messy than many thresholds.

turns.speaker: Zoe Alexander
turns.text: We tested employer views and found many SMEs would support phased rises if given two years’ notice; but the system must avoid complexity that small employers struggle to administer.

turns.speaker: Jack Jones
turns.text: Targeted housing support and making the social security safety net work for pensioners near the pensions credit threshold will do a lot to reduce pensioner poverty.

turns.speaker: Will Sandbrook
turns.text: Trials for non-contingent employer contributions and PAESA pilots would test behaviour and let us pick approaches that don’t create perverse incentives or erosion of the savings norm.

chapters.title: Future risks: self-employment, inequality and sequencing reform
chapters.takeaway: The Commission must consider self-employed coverage, the gender gap, and labour-market change; reform needs a clear timetable, holistic review and sequencing so mitigations accompany rises.

turns.speaker: Rushanara Ali
turns.text: With AI and labour changes, how will inequalities evolve and what should that mean for contribution policy?

turns.speaker: Dr Daniella Jenkins
turns.text: The system is fragile and assumptions may not hold. We need checkpoints and distributional analysis focused on women and vulnerable groups, not just fiscal projections.

turns.speaker: Will Sandbrook
turns.text: Design reforms to work for variable incomes and the self-employed: tax/self-assessment entry points help, but we may need broader ecosystem nudges—banking and accounting tools—to create 'little and often' saving.

turns.speaker: Jack Jones
turns.text: Half of self-employed earn well below median pay; we need options—either a funded collective DC for the self-employed or a small additional state pension funded through additional NICs—to get decent outcomes.

turns.speaker: Damien Egan
turns.text: In what order should changes happen?

turns.speaker: Carl Emmerson
turns.text: Legislate early for a phased timetable, prioritise increasing contributions uniformly, trial new employer-contribution models with big employers, then cautiously lower earnings thresholds.

turns.speaker: Chris Curry
turns.text: Sequence mitigations with the increases: don’t raise contributions first and hope to fix problems later. Give long notice and coordinate with other policies like the national living wage.

turns.speaker: Zoe Alexander
turns.text: Set a clear path to 12% by the early 2030s, but review the lower earnings limit with an independent national council for retirement adequacy to advise on timing and mitigations.

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: Should we trial non-contingent employer contributions and measure employer and worker responses?

turns.speaker: Will Sandbrook
turns.text: Yes—trials and employer consultations are essential to test behaviour, protect the consensus that made the first reforms work, and avoid unintended employer withdrawal from the system.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Final summary from each panel member in one line, please.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Cribb
turns.text: Aim to prevent pensioner poverty and smooth lifetime incomes; be wary of fiscal drag on cash thresholds.

turns.speaker: Chris Curry
turns.text: Raise contributions gradually with long notice, pair increases with practical mitigations and clear objectives.

turns.speaker: Carl Emmerson
turns.text: Automatic enrolment works—use it more, but test new employer contribution approaches and beware timing with wages.

turns.speaker: Zoe Alexander
turns.text: We need higher contributions now and a clear roadmap that protects low earners while improving adequacy.

turns.speaker: Dr Daniella Jenkins
turns.text: Target interventions for women and vulnerable groups, and repurpose regressive tax relief if politically possible.

turns.speaker: Will Sandbrook
turns.text: Combine higher baselines with targeted mitigations: accessible emergency savings, trials, and better support for the self-employed.

turns.speaker: Jack Jones
turns.text: Shift a bigger share of increases to employers, expand collective DC options and strengthen safety-net measures for low-income pensioners.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. The Commission should have concrete options: clearer objectives, higher contribution paths, uprated thresholds, employer support, and tested mitigations for low earners.
